title: Right to privacy as a fundamental right - the practical implications
p1:
Your personal data may be more valuable than you think.

But did you know that in India, the right to privacy is a fundamental right protected by the Constitution?

This recognition goes far beyond keeping your phone password secret.
p2:
Many people assume privacy only matters when they have something to hide. That is a misconception.

In 2017, the Supreme Court of India, in the landmark K.S. Puttaswamy judgment, unanimously recognized privacy as a fundamental right under Article 21 and other freedoms guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution.

In simple terms, your personal choices, communications, bodily autonomy, and personal information deserve constitutional protection against unjustified interference.
p3:
What does this mean in everyday life?

Your private messages, financial details, location data, medical records, and personal choices are not matters that authorities can interfere with arbitrarily. Restrictions on privacy must satisfy constitutional requirements, including legality, a legitimate purpose, and proportionality.

Here is the practical takeaway: before sharing personal information with an app, employer, or service provider, ask what data they collect, why they need it, and how they will use it.

Privacy is not about hiding wrongdoing. It is about retaining control over your personal life and protecting your freedom to make choices without unnecessary intrusion.

A fundamental right matters most when it shapes ordinary decisions, not just courtroom battles.
conclusion: Do you think people in India are sufficiently aware of their constitutional right to privacy, especially when sharing personal data online? What practical privacy protection should everyone know about?
